claim: The innervation of the mammary gland is controlled by brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF).
source: The innervation of the mammary gland is controlled by brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and sexually dimorphic sequestering of BDNF by the truncated form of TrkB (TrkB.T1) directs male-specific axonal pruning in mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work (Liu et al., 2012) and experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Sexually dimorphic sequestering of BDNF by the truncated form of TrkB (TrkB.T1) directs male-specific axonal pruning in mice.
source: The innervation of the mammary gland is controlled by brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and sexually dimorphic sequestering of BDNF by the truncated form of TrkB (TrkB.T1) directs male-specific axonal pruning in mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior work (Liu et al., 2012) and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Specific, non-dimorphic expression of Semaphorin family members was detected in the mouse mammary gland.
source: We detected specific, non-dimorphic, expression of Semaphorin family members in the mouse mammary gland, which signal through PlexinA4.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C-H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Semaphorins in the mammary gland signal through PlexinA4.
source: We detected specific, non-dimorphic, expression of Semaphorin family members in the mouse mammary gland, which signal through PlexinA4.
evidence: This is supported by growth cone collapse assays showing that PlexinA4 deletion abolishes Sema6A and Sema3D responses (Figure 2).

claim: PlexinA4 deletion in both female and male embryos caused developmental hyperinnervation of the mammary gland.
source: PlexinA4 deletion in both female and male embryos caused developmental hyperinnervation of the gland, which could be reduced by genetic co-reduction of BDNF.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Hyperinnervation caused by PlexinA4 deletion could be reduced by genetic co-reduction of BDNF.
source: PlexinA4 deletion in both female and male embryos caused developmental hyperinnervation of the gland, which could be reduced by genetic co-reduction of BDNF.
evidence: This is supported by data from PlexinA4 KO/BDNF Het double mutants shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: In males, PlexinA4 ablation delayed axonal pruning, independently of the initial levels of innervation.
source: Moreover, in males, PlexinA4 ablation delayed axonal pruning, independently of the initial levels of innervation.
evidence: This is supported by data from PlexinA4 KO/BDNF Het males showing delayed pruning despite reduced initial innervation (Figure 5).

claim: In vitro reduction of BDNF induced axonal hypersensitivity to PlexinA4 signaling.
source: In support of this, in vitro reduction of BDNF induced axonal hypersensitivity to PlexinA4 signaling.
evidence: This is supported by growth cone collapse assays showing increased sensitivity to Sema6A in the absence of BDNF (Figure 6).

claim: Precise sensory innervation of the mammary gland is regulated by the balance between trophic and repulsive signaling.
source: Overall, our study shows that precise sensory innervation of the mammary gland is regulated by the balance between trophic and repulsive signaling.
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction experiments showing that BDNF and PlexinA4 have opposing effects on innervation density.

claim: Upon inhibition of trophic signaling, repulsive factors may promote axonal pruning.
source: Upon inhibition of trophic signaling, these repulsive factors may promote axonal pruning.
evidence: This is supported by the delayed pruning phenotype in PlexinA4 KO males and increased sensitivity to Semaphorins when BDNF is reduced.

claim: Sensory neurons of the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) initially extend their axons toward their targets by responding to attractive and repulsive cues expressed in the extracellular environment along their trajectory.
source: Sensory neurons of the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) initially extend their axons toward their targets by responding to attractive and repulsive cues expressed in the extracellular environment along their trajectory (Kolodkin and Tessier-Lavigne, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Once axons reach the targets, limiting amounts of neurotrophic factors control target innervation by regulating axonal growth, neuronal cell death, and pruning.
source: Once axons reach the targets, limiting amounts of neurotrophic factors control target innervation by regulating axonal growth, neuronal cell death, and pruning (Huang and Reichardt, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) acts as a survival factor for specific subsets of sensory neurons during development.
source: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) acts as a survival factor for specific subsets of sensory neurons during development (Kirstein and Fariñas, 2002), and regulates mechanosensation (Carroll et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: BDNF regulates mechanosensation.
source: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) acts as a survival factor for specific subsets of sensory neurons during development (Kirstein and Fariñas, 2002), and regulates mechanosensation (Carroll et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: During early development of the mammary gland, BDNF is required to establish and maintain sensory innervation in both female and male embryos.
source: During early development of the mammary gland, BDNF is required to establish and maintain sensory innervation in both female and male embryos.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2012.

claim: In males only, at later stages of development, sequestering of BDNF by a truncated form of TrkB (TrkB.T1) results in elimination of the axons innervating the gland.
source: In males only, at later stages of development, sequestering of BDNF by a truncated form of TrkB (TrkB.T1) results in elimination of the axons innervating the gland.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2012.

claim: The elimination of axons innervating the male mammary gland is not blocked in the Bax knockout (KO), suggesting that it occurs through axonal pruning rather than cell death.
source: This elimination is not blocked in the Bax knockout (KO), suggesting that it occurs through axonal pruning rather than cell death (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2012.

claim: A sexually dimorphic pattern of mammary gland sensory innervations is formed.
source: As a result, a sexually dimorphic pattern of mammary gland sensory innervations is formed.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2012 and data in Figure 1.

claim: The Semaphorins belong to a large family of secreted and membrane-bound guidance cues.
source: The Semaphorins belong to a large family of secreted and membrane-bound guidance cues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Semaphorins.

claim: The 27 Semaphorin family members are divided into 8 subclasses according to structural homology.
source: The 27 family members are divided into﻿ 8 subclasses according to structural homology (Pasterkamp, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Semaphorins are involved in multiple developmental processes including axonal fasciculation, pruning, dendritic guidance, and modulation of the immune system.
source: Initially characterized for their importance in axonal guidance during development, Semaphorins are now known to be involved in multiple developmental processes including axonal fasciculation, pruning, dendritic guidance, and modulation of the immune system (Pasterkamp and Kolodkin, 2003; Yazdani and Terman, 2006; Tang et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Two receptor families have been implicated in mediating Semaphorin family functions: Plexins and Neuropilins.
source: Two receptor families have been implicated in mediating Semaphorin family functions: Plexins and Neuropilins (Fujisawa and Kitsukawa, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Most class 3 Semaphorins bind to Neuropilins, which associate with type A Plexin family members to transduce their signals through the plasma membrane.
source: Most class 3 Semaphorins bind to Neuropilins, which associate with type A Plexin family members to transduce their signals through the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Semaphorin signaling.

claim: Other members of the Semaphorin family bind and signal directly through Plexin receptors.
source: Other members of the Semaphorin family bind and signal directly through Plexin receptors (Yoshida, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Previous in vitro and overexpression studies demonstrated a crosstalk between class 3 Semaphorins and neurotrophins.
source: Moreover, previous in vitro and overexpression studies demonstrated a crosstalk between class 3 Semaphorins and neurotrophins (Dontchev and Letourneau, 2002; Atwal et al., 2003; Tang et al., 2004; Ben-Zvi et al., 2006; Tang et al., 2007; Ben-Zvi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The sexually dimorphic innervation of the mammary gland at late E13 mouse embryos is a result of differential expression of TrkB.T1 in mesenchymal cells surrounding the mammary epithelium.
source: The sexually dimorphic innervation of the mammary gland at late E13 mouse embryos is a result of differential expression of TrkB.T1 in mesenchymal cells surrounding the mammary epithelium.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2012 and data in Figure 1B.

claim: In male embryos, expression of TrkB.T1 results in sequestering of BDNF, which leads to pruning of the sensory fibers innervating the mammary gland.
source: In male embryos, expression of TrkB.T1 results in sequestering of BDNF, which leads to pruning of the sensory fibers innervating the mammary gland (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2012.

claim: TrkB.T1 is expressed in mesenchymal cells surrounding the mammary epithelium in male embryos.
source: In agreement, we have detected this expression pattern of TrkB.T1 using an antibody that recognizes the TrkB extracellular domain (TrkBECD) (Figure 1B arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TrkB-positive axons innervate the mammary gland in female embryos.
source: In addition, this staining revealed innervation of the gland by TrkB-positive axons in female embryos and reduced innervation in male embryos (Figure 1A,B arrows).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Male embryos show reduced innervation of the mammary gland by TrkB-positive axons compared to females.
source: In addition, this staining revealed innervation of the gland by TrkB-positive axons in female embryos and reduced innervation in male embryos (Figure 1A,B arrows).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Semaphorin3d (Sema3d) is expressed in the epithelial cells of the mammary gland.
source: Our screen detected clear expression of the secreted Semaphorins, Semaphorin3d (Sema3d) and Semaphorin3f (Sema3f), in the epithelial cells of the gland (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Semaphorin3f (Sema3f) is expressed in the epithelial cells of the mammary gland.
source: Our screen detected clear expression of the secreted Semaphorins, Semaphorin3d (Sema3d) and Semaphorin3f (Sema3f), in the epithelial cells of the gland (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: Semaphorin6a (Sema6a) is expressed in the epithelial cells of the mammary gland.
source: Less profound expression of the membrane-bound Semaphorin6a (Sema6a) was detected as well (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1G,H and X-gal staining in Figure 1I,J.

claim: The expression pattern of Sema3d, Sema3f, and Sema6a was identical between female and male embryos.
source: Unlike TrkB.T1 expression, the expression pattern of the three Semaphorins was identical between female and male embryos.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C-J.

claim: Sema6A induces growth cone collapse of BDNF-responsive neurons.
source: Both Sema6A and Sema3D increased this fraction to about 60% of the growth cones.
evidence: This is supported by growth cone collapse assay data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Sema3D induces growth cone collapse of BDNF-responsive neurons.
source: Both Sema6A and Sema3D increased this fraction to about 60% of the growth cones.
evidence: This is supported by growth cone collapse assay data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Sema3F had no effect on growth cone collapse of BDNF-responsive neurons.
source: In contrast, Sema3F had no effect (Figure 2A–F).
evidence: This is supported by growth cone collapse assay data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: PlexinA4 receptor can propagate repulsive activities of both secreted and transmembrane Semaphorins.
source: The PlexinA4 receptor can propagate repulsive activities of both secreted and transmembrane Semaphorins (Suto et al., 2005; Tran et al., 2007; Yoshida, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Sema6A can bind and signal directly through both PlexinA4 or PlexinA2.
source: Sema6A can bind and signal directly through both PlexinA4 or PlexinA2 (Suto et al., 2005; Suto et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: PlexinA4 acts as the signaling co-receptor for Sema3A in a complex with Neuropilin1 (Nrp1).
source: PlexinA4 also acts as the signaling co-receptor for Sema3A in a complex with Neuropilin1 (Nrp1) (Suto et al., 2005; Yaron et al., 2005; Tran et al., 2007; Yoshida, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Sema3D binds Nrp1.
source: While Sema3D was shown to bind Nrp1 (Yazdani and Terman, 2006), the specific Plexin through which it signals was not reported.
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: PlexinA4 serves as the signaling receptor for both Sema6A and Sema3D in BDNF-responsive neurons.
source: Interestingly, we detected complete loss of response both to Sema6A and Sema3D in these neurons (Figure 2A–D), demonstrating that PlexinA4 serves as the signaling receptor for both Sema6A and Sema3D.
evidence: This is supported by growth cone collapse assays using PlexinA4 KO DRGs shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: PlexinA4 is the only binding and signaling receptor for Sema6A in BDNF-responsive neurons of early E13 embryos.
source: In the WT DRGs, a strong signal was detected along the axons, however, no signal was detected in the PlexinA4 KO neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that PlexinA4 is the only binding and signaling receptor for Sema6A in these neurons of early E13 embryos.
evidence: This is supported by Sema6A-Fc binding assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: PlexinA4 mediates axonal growth cone collapse by Sema3D and Sema6A in BDNF-responsive DRG sensory neurons.
source: These in vitro experiments show that PlexinA4 mediates axonal growth cone collapse by Sema3D and Sema6A in BDNF-responsive DRG sensory neurons.
evidence: This is supported by growth cone collapse assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mammary glands of Sema6A KO female embryos are hyperinnervated compared to WT starting at late E13 and continuing to late E14.
source: In female embryos, Tubulin βIII staining (using Tuj1 antibody) showed more axons innervating the gland in Sema6A KO than in WT embryos, beginning at late E13 and continuing to late E14 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Male embryos showed no difference between WT and Sema6A KO in innervation density of the mammary gland.
source: However, male embryos showed no difference between WT and Sema6A KO in innervation density of the gland (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sema6A expressed in the epithelial cells restricts innervation of the mammary gland by sensory axons in females, starting at E13.
source: These results support the idea that Sema6A expressed in the epithelial cells restricts innervation of the gland by the sensory axons in females, starting at E13.
evidence: This is inferred from the hyperinnervation phenotype in Sema6A KO females shown in Figure 3.

claim: PlexinA4 KO female embryos exhibit hyperinnervation of the mammary gland starting at E12 that remained constant at E13 and E14.
source: Compared to WT female embryos, where the fiber density innervating the mammary gland increases gradually during development, in the PlexinA4 KO we detected hyperinnervation of the gland starting at E12 that remained constant at E13 and E14 (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The additional axons in PlexinA4 KO mammary glands are TrkB positive.
source: Importantly, these additional axons appear to be TrkB positive (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: PlexinA4 has a critical role in restricting sensory innervation to the mammary gland during development.
source: These phenotypes were much more severe than the phenotypes we detected in the Sema6A KO (Figure 3), suggesting that PlexinA4 indeed transmits the signaling from additional Semaphorins and has a critical role in restricting sensory innervation to the mammary gland during development.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the severity of phenotypes in PlexinA4 KO versus Sema6A KO.

claim: BDNF produced by the mammary mesenchymal cells promotes the initial ingrowth and maintenance of sensory fibers innervating the gland.
source: It has been shown that BDNF produced by the mammary mesenchymal cells promotes the initial ingrowth and maintenance of sensory fibers innervating the gland (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2012.

claim: The level of nerve growth factor (NGF) limits sensory innervation, such that NGF heterozygous (Het) animals exhibit an altered pattern of sensory projections.
source: It has been previously demonstrated that the level of nerve growth factor (NGF) limits sensory innervation, such that NGF heterozygous (Het) animals exhibit an altered pattern of sensory projections (Crowley et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: BDNF heterozygous (Het) female embryos exhibit a significant reduction in mammary gland innervation at late E12, 13 and 14 compared to WT.
source: Indeed, we observed a significant reduction in mammary gland innervation at late E12, 13 and 14 in BDNF Het embryos compared to WT (Figure 4A,C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A,C.

claim: At late E12, there was no effect on the innervation density of the mammary gland in PlexinA4 KO/BDNF Het compared to PlexinA4 KO.
source: At late E12, there was no effect on the innervation density of the gland compared to PlexinA4 KO (Figure 4A,D), but at later stages, reduction of BDNF levels partially suppressed the hyperinnervation.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A,D.

claim: At late E14, the PlexinA4 KO/BDNF Het exhibited normal mammary gland innervation, indistinguishable from the WT embryos.
source: At late E14, the PlexinA4 KO/BDNF Het exhibited normal mammary gland innervation, indistinguishable from the WT embryos (Figure 4A,D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A,D.

claim: Innervation of the mammary gland is determined by integration of Semaphorins and BDNF pathways in female embryos.
source: These results show that innervation of the mammary gland is determined by integration of Semaphorins and BDNF pathways in female embryos.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: There is a clear developmental decrease in the innervation of WT male mammary glands between late E12 and late E14.
source: As expected, we detected a clear developmental decrease in the innervation of WT male mammary glands between late E12 and late E14 (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: PlexinA4 KO male embryos exhibit hyperinnervation of the mammary gland at late E12.
source: Similar to females, we detected hyperinnervation at late E12 (Figure 5B), suggesting that PlexinA4 signaling restricts the initial innervation of the mammary gland in males as well.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PlexinA4 signaling restricts the initial innervation of the mammary gland in males.
source: Similar to females, we detected hyperinnervation at late E12 (Figure 5B), suggesting that PlexinA4 signaling restricts the initial innervation of the mammary gland in males as well.
evidence: This is inferred from the hyperinnervation phenotype in PlexinA4 KO males at E12.

claim: There was virtually no decrease in fiber density between late E12 and late E13 in the PlexinA4 KO males.
source: Interestingly, there was virtually no decrease in fiber density between late E12 and late E13 in the PlexinA4 KO.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In WT males, fiber density decreased by about 50% between late E12 and late E13.
source: In comparison, in WT males, fiber density decreased by about 50% during the same time frame (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The axons in PlexinA4 KO male mammary glands are TrkB positive.
source: Similar to our results from female embryos, these axons are TrkB positive (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Between late E13 and late E14 there was a sharp decrease in fiber density in the PlexinA4 KO males, but to a level which is still significantly higher than that of WT embryos.
source: Between late E13 and late E14 there was a sharp decrease in fiber density in the PlexinA4 KO, but to a level which is still significantly higher than that of WT embryos.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The delay in pruning in the PlexinA4 KO embryos was not due to lower expression of TrkB.T1.
source: Importantly, the delay in pruning in the PlexinA4 KO embryos was not due to lower expression of TrkB.T1, as we detected similar expression levels in the mesenchymal cells of WT and PlexinA4 KO embryos, using the TrkBECD antibody (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a clear reduction in mammary gland innervation in the BDNF Het male embryos compared to WT at late E12.
source: As in the females, there is a clear reduction in mammary gland innervation in the BDNF Het male embryos compared to WT at late E12 (Figure 5A,C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A,C.

claim: There was a reduction in innervation (~50%) in the PlexinA4 KO/BDNF Het male embryos compared to the PlexinA4 KO, as early as late E12.
source: Unlike in females, we detected a reduction in innervation (~50%) in the PlexinA4 KO/BDNF Het male embryos compared to the PlexinA4 KO, as early as late E12.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Despite greatly reduced initial innervation, there was still a strong delay in axonal elimination between late E12 and late E13 in PlexinA4 KO/BDNF Het males (only 20% decrease).
source: Despite this greatly reduced initial innervation, there was still a strong delay in axonal elimination between late E12 and late E13 (only 20% decrease).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: By late E14, PlexinA4 KO/BDNF Het and PlexinA4 KO male embryos had similar levels of innervation, which was still significantly higher than the WT.
source: By late E14, we detected similar levels of innervation in the PlexinA4 KO/BDNF Het and PlexinA4 KO embryos, which was still significantly higher than the WT (Figure 5A,D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A,D.

claim: PlexinA4 is required for the normal progression of developmental axonal pruning of fibers innervating the male mammary gland.
source: Overall, these results indicate that PlexinA4 is required for the normal progression of developmental axonal pruning of fibers innervating the male mammary gland.
evidence: This is inferred from the delayed pruning phenotype in PlexinA4 KO males shown in Figure 5.

claim: Using in vitro growth cone collapse assays with low levels of BDNF resulted in hypersensitivity to PlexinA4 signaling.
source: Using in vitro growth cone collapse assays with low levels of BDNF resulted in hypersensitivity to PlexinA4 signaling, showing that inhibition of BDNF signaling renders the axons more sensitive to PlexinA4.
evidence: This is supported by growth cone collapse assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the presence of BDNF, low concentration of Sema6A (0.025 ng/µl) did not induce growth cone collapse.
source: In the presence of BDNF, this concentration of Sema6A did not induce growth cone collapse.
evidence: This is supported by growth cone collapse assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Adding Sema6A at low concentration (0.025 ng/µl) to media without BDNF resulted in 60% growth cone collapse.
source: However, adding Sema6A at this concentration to the -BDNF media resulted in 60% growth cone collapse (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by growth cone collapse assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: At low levels of BDNF, sensory axons become hypersensitive to PlexinA4 signaling, which results in more collapsed growth cones.
source: This demonstrates that at low levels of BDNF, sensory axons become hypersensitive to PlexinA4 signaling, which results in more collapsed growth cones.
evidence: This is inferred from the growth cone collapse assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: BDNF inhibits the Semaphorin signaling.
source: These results support the idea that BDNF inhibits the Semaphorin signaling, and may suggest that upon BDNF sequestering the axons become hypersensitive to PlexinA4 signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro data showing increased sensitivity to Semaphorins when BDNF is removed.

claim: Upon BDNF sequestering the axons become hypersensitive to PlexinA4 signaling.
source: These results support the idea that BDNF inhibits the Semaphorin signaling, and may suggest that upon BDNF sequestering the axons become hypersensitive to PlexinA4 signaling.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the in vitro data.

claim: There was no significant difference in innervation between the PlexinA4/TrkB.T1 double KO and the PlexinA4 single KO at E13 or E14.
source: There was no significant difference in innervation between the double KO and the PlexinA4 single KO at E13 or E14.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7.

claim: TrkB.T1 and PlexinA4 operate in parallel and converge to the same axonal elimination pathway.
source: Overall, these results are consistent with the idea that TrkB.T1 and PlexinA4 operate in parallel and converge to the same axonal elimination pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of additive effect in the double KO shown in Figure 7.

claim: In the TrkB.T1 single KO at E13, the level of innervation is higher than the WT due to decreased pruning.
source: In the TrkB.T1 single KO at E13, the level of innervation is higher than the WT due to decreased pruning, as previously demonstrated by Liu et al.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7 and citation to Liu et al.

claim: At E14, the level of innervation in TrkB.T1 KO dropped to WT levels.
source: However, at E14, the level of innervation dropped to WT levels.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The process of target innervation by sensory axons during embryonic development is largely regulated by neurotrophic factors secreted by the target in limited amounts.
source: The process of target innervation by sensory axons during embryonic development is largely regulated by neurotrophic factors secreted by the target in limited amounts.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Studies of NGF have demonstrated a strong correlation between its expression and the innervation density of the skin.
source: Studies of NGF have demonstrated a strong correlation between its expression and the innervation density of the skin (Davies et al., 1987), and that overexpression of NGF results in hyperinnervation of the target organ (Albers et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Overexpression of NGF results in hyperinnervation of the target organ.
source: Studies of NGF have demonstrated a strong correlation between its expression and the innervation density of the skin (Davies et al., 1987), and that overexpression of NGF results in hyperinnervation of the target organ (Albers et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: There is growing evidence that additional target-derived cues are involved in specifying innervation, some through interaction with the neurotrophin signaling pathways.
source: However, there is growing evidence that additional target-derived cues are involved in specifying innervation, some through interaction with the neurotrophin signaling pathways (Guha et al., 2004; Bäumer et al., 2014; Wheeler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The mammary gland serves as a unique model for sexually dimorphic target innervation controlled by BDNF.
source: The mammary gland serves as a unique model for sexually dimorphic target innervation controlled by BDNF, but whether other factors regulate this process jointly with BDNF was not known.
evidence: This is established from prior work and the current study.

claim: A critical role for the Semaphorin-PlexinA4 signaling pathway in axonal innervation restriction and possibly pruning promotion was discovered.
source: Through the studies described here, we discovered a critical role for the Semaphorin-PlexinA4 signaling pathway in axonal innervation restriction and possibly pruning promotion.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental data.

claim: The Androgen receptor is not expressed in DRG neurons.
source: Since the Androgen receptor is not expressed in DRG neurons (Liu et al., 2012), it is likely that PlexinA4 is expressed in non-dimorphic manner as well.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2012.

claim: PlexinA4 is likely expressed in non-dimorphic manner in DRG neurons.
source: Since the Androgen receptor is not expressed in DRG neurons (Liu et al., 2012), it is likely that PlexinA4 is expressed in non-dimorphic manner as well.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of androgen receptor expression in DRG neurons.

claim: Although BDNF is expressed in limited amounts, its physiological levels are sufficient to sustain high levels of innervation, which are curbed by Semaphorin signaling.
source: These results suggest that although BDNF is expressed in limited amounts, its physiological levels are sufficient to sustain high levels of innervation, which are curbed by Semaphorin signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction experiments in females.

claim: Male axons may have an intrinsic hypersensitivity to BDNF levels, which is only revealed on the background of PlexinA4 KO.
source: The basis for this difference is currently unclear, however, it may reflect an intrinsic hypersensitivity of the male axons to BDNF levels, which is only revealed on the background of PlexinA4 KO.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning to explain the observed difference between males and females.

claim: The hypersensitivity of male axons to BDNF may help to promote pruning once BDNF is sequestered.
source: This hypersensitivity may help to promote pruning once BDNF is sequestered.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed phenotypes.

claim: Ablation of PlexinA4 does not affect the expression of TrkB.T1.
source: Lastly, while our results show that ablation of PlexinA4 does not affect the expression of TrkB.T1, we were not able to visualize BDNF at the gland by immunostaining.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Growth cone collapse is an early and critical step in axonal degeneration in response to trophic deprivation.
source: Although this assay is mainly correlated with growth inhibition by the Semaphorins and not axonal pruning, a recent study suggested that growth cone collapse is an early and critical step in axonal degeneration in response to trophic deprivation (Unsain et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Unsain et al., 2018.

claim: The hypersensitivity to PlexinA4-induced growth cone collapse may reflect promotion of the pruning process.
source: Therefore, the hypersensitivity to PlexinA4-induced growth cone collapse may reflect promotion of the pruning process.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the in vitro data and citation to Unsain et al., 2018.

claim: BDNF counteracts PlexinA4 effects.
source: Interestingly, while BDNF counteracts PlexinA4 effects, our results suggest that PlexinA4 and the BDNF receptor isoform TrkB.T1 operate in the same pathway of axonal elimination, since co-ablation of the two did not have any additive effect.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction experiments.

claim: TrkB.T1 antagonizes BDNF signaling in the mammary gland.
source: This result supports previous data that TrkB.T1 antagonizes BDNF signaling in the mammary gland (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2012 and data from the double KO experiment.

claim: Neither ablation of PlexinA4 or of TrkB.T1 was able to prevent pruning at late E14, when the innervation density drops sharply.
source: Nevertheless, neither ablation of PlexinA4 or of TrkB.T1 was able to prevent pruning at late E14, when the innervation density drops sharply.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7.

claim: During mammary organogenesis, the mammary gland of male embryos starts to regress as a result of Androgen release by the male gonads at E13.
source: During mammary organogenesis, the mammary gland of male embryos starts to regress as a result of Androgen release by the male gonads at E13 (Robinson, 2007), and this regression probably forces elimination of the axons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Robinson, 2007.

claim: Mammary gland regression in males probably forces elimination of the axons.
source: During mammary organogenesis, the mammary gland of male embryos starts to regress as a result of Androgen release by the male gonads at E13 (Robinson, 2007), and this regression probably forces elimination of the axons.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the timing of gland regression and axonal elimination.

claim: Developmental innervation of the mammary gland is regulated by a balance between BDNF, which promotes the initial ingrowth of the sensory fibers, and constant Semaphorin signaling, which restricts innervation.
source: Altogether, our study shows that developmental innervation of the mammary gland is regulated by a balance between BDNF, which promotes the initial ingrowth of the sensory fibers, and constant Semaphorin signaling, which restricts innervation (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all experimental data.

claim: Upon inhibition of BDNF-TrkB signaling, Semaphorin-PlexinA4 signaling may promote axonal pruning.
source: Upon inhibition of BDNF-TrkB signaling, Semaphorin-PlexinA4 signaling may promote axonal pruning (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the delayed pruning phenotype in PlexinA4 KO males and in vitro data.

claim: A previous in vitro study has demonstrated that the class 3 Semaphorins inhibit neurotrophin signaling and that this inhibition is a part of the mechanism by which they induce growth cone collapse.
source: A previous in vitro study has demonstrated that the class 3 Semaphorins inhibit neurotrophin signaling and that this inhibition is a part of the mechanism by which they induce growth cone collapse (Atwal et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Atwal et al., 2003.

claim: Neurotrophins signaling suppresses the Semaphorin signaling, and once this suppression is relieved, the axons become hypersensitive to Semaphorins.
source: Our results also support the idea that neurotrophins signaling suppresses the Semaphorin signaling, and once this suppression is relieved, the axons become hypersensitive to Semaphorins, as was proposed by Dontchev and Letourneau (Dontchev and Letourneau, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by the in vitro data and citation to Dontchev and Letourneau, 2002.

claim: The balance between BDNF and Semaphorins plays a role in accurate wiring of the nervous system during development.
source: Overall, our work provides the first clear evidence that the balance between these two cues plays a role in accurate wiring of the nervous system during development, and that physiologically tipping this balance may induce axonal pruning.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Physiologically tipping the balance between BDNF and Semaphorins may induce axonal pruning.
source: Overall, our work provides the first clear evidence that the balance between these two cues plays a role in accurate wiring of the nervous system during development, and that physiologically tipping this balance may induce axonal pruning.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing delayed pruning in PlexinA4 KO males.

claim: The Semaphorins have been previously implicated in pruning of hippocampal axons, where developmental expression of Sema3F was proposed to largely regulate this process.
source: The Semaphorins have been previously implicated in pruning of hippocampal axons, where developmental expression of Sema3F was proposed to largely regulate this process (Bagri et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bagri et al., 2003.

claim: In the mammary gland, there is no dimorphic or temporal expression of Semaphorins or PlexinA4.
source: In contrast, in the mammary gland, we did not detect any dimorphic or temporal expression of Semaphorins or PlexinA4; instead, our results suggest that their ability to prune axons in male embryos is gated by inhibition of BDNF signaling.
evidence: This is supported by the in situ hybridization data in Figure 1.

claim: The ability of Semaphorins to prune axons in male embryos is gated by inhibition of BDNF signaling.
source: In contrast, in the mammary gland, we did not detect any dimorphic or temporal expression of Semaphorins or PlexinA4; instead, our results suggest that their ability to prune axons in male embryos is gated by inhibition of BDNF signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing delayed pruning in PlexinA4 KO males and increased sensitivity to Semaphorins when BDNF is reduced.

claim: Expression of Semaphorins and Plexins has been previously demonstrated in the developing mammary gland postnatally, and was suggested to affect ductal growth and morphogenesis of the gland.
source: Expression of Semaphorins and Plexins has been previously demonstrated in the developing mammary gland postnatally, and was suggested to affect ductal growth and morphogenesis of the gland (Morris et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Morris et al., 2006.

claim: Sema3D and Sema6A are expressed in the mammary epithelium during embryonic development.
source: Here we present new data that show expression of Sema3D and Sema6A in the mammary epithelium during embryonic development, and their involvement in regulation of the mammary gland innervation through the PlexinA4 receptor.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 1.

claim: Sema3D and Sema6A are involved in regulation of the mammary gland innervation through the PlexinA4 receptor.
source: Here we present new data that show expression of Sema3D and Sema6A in the mammary epithelium during embryonic development, and their involvement in regulation of the mammary gland innervation through the PlexinA4 receptor.
evidence: This is supported by the growth cone collapse assays and in vivo phenotypes.

claim: Sema3F is expressed in the mammary epithelium.
source: We also detected expression of Sema3F in the mammary epithelium, but in vitro it had no effect on growth cone collapse of BDNF-responsive sensory neurons, suggesting it is not involved in target innervation.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 1.

claim: Sema3F had no effect on growth cone collapse of BDNF-responsive sensory neurons, suggesting it is not involved in target innervation.
source: We also detected expression of Sema3F in the mammary epithelium, but in vitro it had no effect on growth cone collapse of BDNF-responsive sensory neurons, suggesting it is not involved in target innervation.
evidence: This is supported by growth cone collapse assay data in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Sema3F may have a role in the regulation of ductal directional outgrowth and branching morphogenesis during later development.
source: It may have a role in the regulation of ductal directional outgrowth and branching morphogenesis during later development.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the expression pattern and known functions of Sema3F.

claim: Neuropilin2, which serves as the binding receptor of Sema3F, promotes postnatal branching morphogenesis of the mammary gland.
source: This is supported by the fact that Neuropilin2, which serves as the binding receptor of Sema3F (Yoshida, 2012), promotes postnatal branching morphogenesis of the mammary gland (Goel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yoshida, 2012 and Goel et al., 2011.

claim: The Semaphorins play a dual role in mammary gland development, determining the extent of sensory innervation density prenatally and promoting gland morphogenesis postnatally.
source: Together, these results suggest that the Semaphorins play a dual role in mammary gland development, determining the extent of sensory innervation density prenatally and promoting gland morphogenesis postnatally.
evidence: This is inferred from the current study and prior literature.

claim: The neurotrophins and the Semaphorins continue to be expressed in peripheral tissues throughout the life of the organism.
source: Intriguingly, the neurotrophins and the Semaphorins continue to be expressed in peripheral tissues throughout the life of the organism, and their expression may be altered in pathological conditions (Apfel, 1999; Yamaguchi et al., 2008; Tominaga et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Expression of neurotrophins and Semaphorins may be altered in pathological conditions.
source: Intriguingly, the neurotrophins and the Semaphorins continue to be expressed in peripheral tissues throughout the life of the organism, and their expression may be altered in pathological conditions (Apfel, 1999; Yamaguchi et al., 2008; Tominaga et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Altered expression of neurotrophins and Semaphorins could induce aberrant innervation in mature animals, causing either hypersensitivity or reduced sensation, depending on the balance between these pathways.
source: Our findings raise the possibility that altered expression of these cues could induce aberrant innervation in mature animals, causing either hypersensitivity or reduced sensation, depending on the balance between these pathways.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the findings of the study.
